caption: The little tarmac lane along the Old Road Triangle, with white timber marker posts and dense overgrown hedgerow on the right. The undergrowth is exactly the kind of cover that supports the bird list we hear in here in summer (Wren, Blackcap, Chiffchaff, Goldcrest and the rest). Untouched since the N75 was rerouted in 2010 (May 2026)

Looking down through the canopy at the Old Road Triangle. Hazel and Hawthorn arch right over the ground and turn the whole space into a green tunnel. Nobody has touched this since 2010 and it shows: a proper little wildlife refuge inside the village edge (May 2026)

A mature multi-stemmed Hazel coppice on the Old Road Triangle. This is exactly the kind of structure that takes decades to build and seconds to destroy, and it's the single best argument for the no-touch policy on this piece of ground. Hazel supports a huge range of wildlife from dormice to nesting birds to early-spring catkin pollinators (May 2026)

Spanish Bluebells in flower right alongside Stinging Nettles at the Old Road Triangle in early May. The upright stem with bells coming off all sides (rather than the one-sided drooping curve of the native bluebell) is the giveaway. The Stinging Nettle is a workhorse pollinator host plant for caterpillars of Small Tortoiseshell, Peacock and Red Admiral butterflies. Honest, untouched, doing its job (May 2026)
